questions.question: What are the five recurring risk categories common across AI programs, according to this lesson?
options: Marketing, sales, legal, HR, and finance risk
Quality, cost, latency, security, and dependency risk
Only cost and latency risk — the other categories don't apply to AI
Weather, geopolitics, currency, supply chain, and labor risk
questions.explanation: These five categories (quality, cost, latency, security, dependency) recur across nearly every AI program and map directly to concepts covered throughout this curriculum.

questions.question: How does 'likelihood x impact' scoring help prioritize risk mitigation effort?
options: It ensures every risk gets exactly equal mitigation effort regardless of severity
It ranks risks so that high-likelihood, high-impact risks are mitigated first, rather than spreading effort evenly across all risks regardless of severity
It only measures cost, ignoring all other risk types
It is used only after an incident has already occurred
questions.explanation: Multiplying likelihood by impact produces a priority score that helps focus limited mitigation effort on the risks most likely to cause serious harm, rather than treating all identified risks as equally urgent.

questions.question: A program hits cost overruns, a quality regression, and a rate-limit outage within its first month — all things this curriculum identifies as well-known risk categories. Which question best addresses the root process gap?
options: Should we conclude these were simply unpredictable bad luck?
Did we identify and score these risks in a risk register before launch, or did we discover each one only as a live incident?
Should we abandon the AI program entirely after these issues?
Is this an unavoidable cost of building AI products?
questions.explanation: None of these risks were genuinely unpredictable — they fall into well-known categories. The gap is a missing proactive risk register that would have surfaced and prioritized mitigation for these risks before they became incidents.
